speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the nature of your vertigo—does the room seem to be spinning around you, or do you feel like you are swaying or losing your balance?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the vertigo recur if you move your head in specific directions, such as rolling over in bed or looking up? Are you experiencing any hearing loss, tinnitus, or a feeling of fullness in your ears?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness.

speaker: Doctor
text: Did the spinning sensation return when you tried to get back into bed or change your head position after the initial episode? Also, did you notice any ringing in your ears or hearing loss during that time?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any difficulty speaking, weakness in your limbs, or facial drooping? I need to rule out a central cause like a stroke given your age and sudden onset.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

speaker: Doctor
text:
REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver

REQUEST TEST: MRI Brain

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient’s symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back. MRI Brain: Normal, with no evidence of stroke or masses.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the left side, combined with the normal MRI and absence of other neurological symptoms, strongly points to a peripheral cause. Based on these findings, I am confident in my assessment.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
